questions.q: According to the four-question framework in this lesson, what should you check first when facing a new requirement?
options: Whether it can be handled with one SQL statement, such as a view or a scheduled Task
Whether an orchestrator like Airflow is available
Whether Python has a library for it
Whether dbt has a pre-built model for it
questions.explain: The framework starts with the simplest sufficient option — if plain SQL solves it, that's the whole answer, with no additional tool needed.

questions.q: In Scenario B (forty transformation models built by a five-person team needing tests, docs, and version history), why is dbt recommended over plain SQL alone?
options: dbt formalizes the SQL with tests, documentation, and version control — not because the SQL itself is more complex
dbt can execute logic that SQL cannot, such as calling REST APIs
dbt replaces the need for a Snowflake warehouse entirely
Plain SQL cannot be used by more than one team member
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that dbt doesn't do anything SQL couldn't already do — it adds discipline (tests, docs, version control) around SQL for team-scale reuse.

questions.q: In Scenario C (pulling daily currency exchange rates from a third-party REST API), which tool does this lesson recommend, and why?
options: Python, because no amount of SQL can call an external API
dbt, because it can natively call REST APIs
An orchestrator alone, with no other tool needed
A Snowflake resource monitor, since this is a cost concern
questions.explain: Calling an external API requires logic SQL fundamentally cannot express, which is exactly the case this lesson assigns to Python via Snowpark or a connector.

questions.q: In Scenario D (an ADF load must finish before dbt runs, and a Python step must finish before a Power BI refresh), what is the actual problem being solved?
options: Sequencing and dependency across multiple systems, which is an orchestrator's job
Writing more complex SQL transformations
Choosing a bigger Snowflake warehouse size
Formatting the Power BI report itself
questions.explain: Each individual step might already be solved by another tool; the orchestrator's job is purely making sure step order is respected and failures are surfaced.

questions.q: What 'other mistake' does this lesson warn against, beyond under-using tools?
options: Reaching for extra tools 'just in case' — e.g. standing up dbt or an orchestrator for a problem plain SQL already solves
Using too much SQL instead of Python
Refusing to ever use Airflow under any circumstances
Documenting SQL views instead of leaving them undocumented
questions.explain: Adding unnecessary tools increases operational surface area — maintenance, monitoring, onboarding — for a problem that a simpler solution already handled.
